Quantiles Equivalence Testing (2026)

Source: vignettes/articles/reproducibility-quantile.Rmd
reproducibility-quantile.Rmd

This document describes how to reproduce the simulations and case studies in Wu, J., Guerrier, S., Gou, S., Kalia, Y. N., and Insolia, L. (2026), Bridging the gap between experimental burden and statistical power for quantiles equivalence testing. The methods are implemented in the cTOST R package through qtost() and compare_to_qtost(); see the Quantile Equivalence Testing article for an introduction.

The reproducibility material is provided in reproducibility/quantile/, and all paths below are relative to this path. The analyses used cTOST version 1.1.0.

Simulation studies

The simulation studies were run on the University of Geneva’s HPC infrastructure. Each study used 50,000 Monte Carlo replications, split across 5,000 single-CPU array tasks, with 10 replications per task. The submission scripts use Bash and Slurm. Before running them on another cluster, adapt the module-loading commands, partition and resource requests (see launch.sh and recomb.sh below). Also ensure that cTOST and tictoc are installed in the cluster’s R environment.

Single quantile

The single-quantile simulation study compares the rejection rates of qTOST and α\alpha-qTOST across reference quantiles, equivalence margins, sample sizes and variance ratios. The source code is in simulations/HPC/sim_univ/. Namely:

File Purpose
sim_options.R Defines the statistical design and calibration controls.
sim_HPC_main.R Runs assigned replications and saves test decisions.
out_HPC_combine.R Validates results and computes rejection probabilities.
setting.sh Sets study, replication/task counts and output paths.
all.sh Submits the array and schedules aggregation on success.
launch.sh Loads the cluster R environment and starts an array task.
recomb.sh Runs the R aggregation script and then cleanup.
clean.sh Removes chunks and logs after verifying aggregation.

Simulation setting 1: size

Setting 1 evaluates rejection rates at the two equivalence boundaries, πy=πx−δ\pi_y = \pi_x - \delta and πx+δ\pi_x + \delta, to compare the test size for the two procedures and reproduce Figure 3. The results can be reproduced as follows:

export n_simu=50000 n_array=5000
sim_setting=1 bash simulations/HPC/sim_univ/all.sh

The inline sim_setting=1 selects the study without editing setting.sh. The all.sh script submits the aggregation job, recomb.sh, with a dependency on successful completion of the simulation array. After aggregation succeeds, clean.sh removes the temporary replication chunks and individual task logs, while retaining the combined results. The submission scripts refuse to reuse a nonempty output directory (so keep previous outputs separately before rerunning the same setting).

Once the job is completed, the combined results are saved in:

simulations/HPC/sim_univ/sim_HPC_out/sim_setting_1/
  results_sim_setting_size_1_n_simu_50000_n_array_5000.rdata

This file contains sol_TOST_avg and sol_alphaTOST_avg, the estimated rejection probabilities (expressed as percentages) for qTOST and α\alpha-qTOST, respectively. Both are 4 x 3 x 4 x 2 x 2 arrays, indexed by nyn_y, nx/nyn_x/n_y, quantile/margin pair, variance ratio and equivalence boundary. For example, inspect the results with:

load(paste0("simulations/HPC/sim_univ/sim_HPC_out/sim_setting_1/",
            "results_sim_setting_size_1_n_simu_50000_n_array_5000.rdata"))
dim(sol_TOST_avg)
dimnames(sol_TOST_avg)
range(sol_alphaTOST_avg - sol_TOST_avg)

The last command gives the range of differences in rejection rates, in percentage points. The aggregation report, report_recomb_HPC.Rout, is retained in the same sim_setting_1/ output directory.

Then, to reproduce Figure 3, run:

source("simulations/fig_3_heatmap_diff_size.R")

For each design and procedure, the figure displays the larger rejection percentage at the two simulated boundaries, with a Monte Carlo tolerance band around the nominal level of 5%.

By default, tikzPlot = 0 generates figures on the active R graphics device. To regenerate the publication-style files, set tikzPlot = 1 inside each plotting script before sourcing it, and install tikzDevice plus a working LaTeX distribution. Create the tex/ subfolder if needed, so that each generated .tex file can then be compiled to PDF. For instance:

install.packages("tikzDevice")
dir.create("tex", showWarnings = FALSE)
latexmk -pdf -outdir=tex tex/fig3.tex

Simulation setting 2: power and type-I error

Setting 2 uses the same job submission, aggregation and cleanup workflow. It evaluates rejection probabilities over 50 equally spaced values of θ=Φ−1(πy)\theta = \Phi^{-1}(\pi_y), from Φ−1(πx−1.2δ)\Phi^{-1}(\pi_x - 1.2\delta) to Φ−1(πx+1.2δ)\Phi^{-1}(\pi_x + 1.2\delta), covering the equivalence region and nearby null values. In this case, keep the same n_simu and n_array values and change the Bash variable sim_setting:

export n_simu=50000 n_array=5000
sim_setting=2 bash simulations/HPC/sim_univ/all.sh

After aggregation, the output file is:

simulations/HPC/sim_univ/sim_HPC_out/sim_setting_2/
  results_sim_setting_2_n_simu_50000_n_array_5000.rdata

It contains the same two objects, sol_TOST_avg and sol_alphaTOST_avg, with the same units and dimension order. The last dimension now indexes 50 grid positions, giving 4 x 3 x 4 x 2 x 50 arrays. To reproduce the original Figures 1–2 and S1–S6, run:

source("simulations/fig_1_heatmap_diff_pow.R")  # Figures 1 and S1
source("simulations/fig_2_power_curves.R")      # Figures 2 and S2-S6

Figures 1 and S1 show the gain of α\alpha-qTOST over qTOST in percentage points. Figures 2 and S2–S6 show the curves against πy\pi_y, with the nominal level and equivalence limits as reference lines.

Multiple quantiles

The multiple-quantile simulation study compares the rejection rates of qTOST and α\alpha-qTOST when assessing two reference quantiles jointly. The source code is in simulations/HPC/sim_mvt/. This follows the same workflow and code structure as the single-quantile setup presented above.

Here, the two reference quantile levels πx=(0.20,0.80)\pi_x = (0.20, 0.80) are assessed jointly, with margin δ=0.15\delta = 0.15, and the overall declaration of equivalence requires both quantile assessments to be satisfied. Variance ratio γ=1\gamma=1 and nominal level α=0.05\alpha=0.05 were considered in this study, which evaluates a 50×5050 \times 50 grid of transformed parameter pairs θ1\theta_1 and θ2\theta_2. The design and calibration settings are defined in this directory’s sim_options.R.

The variable sim_setting determines the sample size:

sim_setting Observations per group Figure
1 30 4
2 10 S7
3 50 S8

To reproduce the simulation results, run:

export n_simu=50000 n_array=5000
sim_setting=1 bash simulations/HPC/sim_mvt/all.sh
sim_setting=2 bash simulations/HPC/sim_mvt/all.sh
sim_setting=3 bash simulations/HPC/sim_mvt/all.sh

The combined results are saved separately for each setting, namely:

simulations/HPC/sim_mvt/sim_HPC_out/sim_setting_1/
  results_mvt_sim_setting_1_n_simu_50000_n_array_5000.rdata
  
simulations/HPC/sim_mvt/sim_HPC_out/sim_setting_2/
  results_mvt_sim_setting_2_n_simu_50000_n_array_5000.rdata

simulations/HPC/sim_mvt/sim_HPC_out/sim_setting_3/
  results_mvt_sim_setting_3_n_simu_50000_n_array_5000.rdata

Each file contains sol_TOST_avg and sol_piTOST_avg, the rejection probabilities for qTOST and α\alpha-qTOST, respectively. These are 50 x 50 matrices, with rows indexing the second transformed parameter and columns indexing the first.

Once all three combined results are available, Figures 4, S7 and S8 can be obtained by running:

source("simulations/fig_4_pow_heatmap_mvt.R")

Each figure displays the rejection probabilities of the two procedures across the parameter grid, their difference, and histograms of rejection rates on the equivalence-region boundary.

Case studies

The source code to reproduce the two case studies is provided in case_study/. The full analyses were run locally using R version 4.4.3, and took around 2 minutes in total on a standard laptop.

Case study 1: A bridging clinical trial across gender populations

The first case study compares plasma trough concentrations of tipranavir between male and female patients using summary statistics from Table 5 of the FDA drug label. The reference group comprises 106 male patients, and the test group comprises 14 female patients.

Assuming lognormal concentrations, the log-scale means and standard deviations were reconstructed by moment matching. The complete analysis is in case_study/case_study_hiv.R. It evaluates 191 reference quantile levels from 0.11 to 0.30 in steps of 0.001, at nominal level 0.05 and margin 0.10.

To reproduce the original analysis, run:

source("case_study/case_study_hiv.R")  # Figures 5 and 6

The results are stored in the 191 x 3 matrices res and res_star for qTOST and α\alpha-qTOST, respectively. Rows index reference quantile levels, and columns give the lower interval endpoint, estimated probability and upper endpoint. Figure 5 displays the results at two (separately assessed) quantile reference levels πx=0.15\pi_x=0.15 and πx=0.20\pi_x=0.20. Figure 6 shows intervals across a larger range. Also in this case, set tikzPlot = 1 inside the script to write tex/fig5.tex and tex/fig6.tex, then compile them as described above.

As an illustration, Figure 5 can be reproduced as follows.

First load and transform the data:

# Original-scale means, standard deviations and sample sizes
mu_x = 35.6
sd_x = 16.7
n_x = 106
mu_y = 41.6
sd_y = 24.3
n_y = 14

# Log-scale summaries
x = list(mean = log(mu_x^2 / sqrt(mu_x^2 + sd_x^2)),
         sd = sqrt(log(1 + sd_x^2 / mu_x^2)), n = n_x)
y = list(mean = log(mu_y^2 / sqrt(mu_y^2 + sd_y^2)),
         sd = sqrt(log(1 + sd_y^2 / mu_y^2)), n = n_y)

Then specify the designs and obtain the qTOST and the α\alpha-qTOST assessments:

library(cTOST)

pi_x = c(0.15, 0.20)
alpha = 0.05
delta = 0.10

hiv_qtost = lapply(pi_x, function(p) {
  qtost(x, y, pi_x = p, delta = delta, alpha = alpha,
        method = "unadjusted")
})

hiv_alpha_qtost = lapply(pi_x, function(p) {
  qtost(x, y, pi_x = p, delta = delta, alpha = alpha,
        method = "alpha", B = 100000, seed = 12345,
        tol = .Machine$double.eps)
})

The results at each reference quantile can also be compared directly:

compare_to_qtost(hiv_alpha_qtost[[1]])  # 15th percentile
#> qTOST: ✖ Can't accept quantile (bio)equivalence
#> alpha-qTOST: ✖ Can't accept quantile (bio)equivalence
#> 
#> Equiv. Region:   |------------------------|       
#> qTOST:          (--------------x------------------)
#> alpha-qTOST:      (------------x------------)      
#> 
#>                CI - low      CI - high
#> qTOST:         0.05208       0.31514
#> alpha-qTOST:   0.07011       0.26390
#> 
#> Equiv. lim. = dw/up 0.05000 0.25000
compare_to_qtost(hiv_alpha_qtost[[2]])  # 20th percentile
#> qTOST: ✖ Can't accept quantile (bio)equivalence
#> alpha-qTOST: ✔ Accept quantile (bio)equivalence
#> 
#> Equiv. Region:      |---------------------|       
#> qTOST:          (--------------x------------------)
#> alpha-qTOST:       (-----------x----------)        
#> 
#>                CI - low      CI - high
#> qTOST:         0.07568       0.36283
#> alpha-qTOST:   0.10857       0.29065
#> 
#> Equiv. lim. = dw/up 0.10000 0.30000

Finally, display the confidence intervals and equivalence margins:

plot_intervals = function(qtost_fit, alpha_qtost_fit, pi_x, delta,
                          k = 1, xlim, main) {
  ci = rbind(qtost_fit$ci[k, ], alpha_qtost_fit$ci[k, ])
  estimate = c(qtost_fit$pi_y_hat[k], alpha_qtost_fit$pi_y_hat[k])
  cols = c("#501d8a", "#ee8c7d")
  ypos = c(2, 1)

  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0.4, 2.7), axes = FALSE,
       xlab = expression(pi[y]), ylab = "", main = main)
  rect(pi_x - delta, 0.4, pi_x + delta, 2.7,
       col = adjustcolor("#FF9900", alpha.f = 0.15), border = NA)
  abline(h = ypos, col = "grey85")
  abline(v = pi_x, col = "grey65", lty = 3)
  abline(v = pi_x + c(-delta, delta), lty = 3)
  arrows(ci[, 1], ypos, ci[, 2], ypos, angle = 90, code = 3,
         length = 0.07, col = cols, lwd = 2.5)
  points(estimate, ypos, pch = 16, col = cols, cex = 1.5)
  axis(1)
  axis(2, at = ypos, labels = expression("qTOST", alpha*"-qTOST"),
       las = 1, tick = FALSE)
}

old_par = par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 5.5, 2.5, 1), yaxs = "i")

for (i in seq_along(pi_x)) {
  plot_intervals(hiv_qtost[[i]], hiv_alpha_qtost[[i]],
                 pi_x = pi_x[i], delta = delta, xlim = c(0, 0.4),
                 main = bquote(pi[x] == .(pi_x[i])))
}
par(old_par)

While neither procedure establishes equivalence at the 15th percentile, the α\alpha-qTOST interval is entirely inside the equivalence margins and establishes equivalence at the 20th percentile when the qTOST fails to do so.

Case study 2: Demonstrating inter-operator reproducibility

The second case study compares the cutaneous delivery of a compound measured by two operators using the same experimental protocol. The biodistribution dataset contains six independent observations per operator. Its X and Y columns are already on the logarithmic scale and represent the reference and test operators, respectively.

The complete analysis is in case_study/case_study_lad_mvt.R, which jointly tests the 20th and 80th reference percentiles over 20 nominal significance levels from 0.01 to 0.20, with margin 0.15. This follows the same workflow as the one described for the first case study. To reproduce the complete analysis, run:

source("case_study/case_study_lad_mvt.R")  # Figures 7 and 8

The results are stored in sol_qtost and sol_alpha_qtost, each a 2 x 3 x 20 array indexed by reference quantile, lower endpoint/estimate/upper endpoint, and nominal level. Figure 7 displays the significance levels 0.05 and 0.10. Figure 8 shows intervals across a larger range.

As an illustration, Figure 7 can be reproduced as follows.

First load the data:

library(cTOST)

data(biodistribution)
x = biodistribution$X
y = biodistribution$Y

Then jointly assess the two reference quantiles at nominal significance levels 0.05 and 0.10. The designs and the qTOST and the α\alpha-qTOST assessments can be obtained as follows:

pi_x = c(0.2, 0.8)
delta = 0.15
alphas = c(0.05, 0.1)

lad_qtost = lapply(alphas, function(a) {
  qtost(x, y, pi_x = pi_x, delta = delta, alpha = a,
        method = "unadjusted")
})

lad_alpha_qtost = lapply(alphas, function(a) {
  qtost(x, y, pi_x = pi_x, delta = delta, alpha = a,
        method = "alpha", B = 10000, seed = 12345,
        tol = sqrt(.Machine$double.eps), max_iter = 5,
        tolpower = 1e-3, MC_sup = TRUE)
})

Finally, display the confidence intervals and equivalence margins, with reference quantiles in columns and nominal levels in rows:

plot_intervals = function(qtost_fit, alpha_qtost_fit, pi_x, delta,
                          k = 1, xlim, main) {
  ci = rbind(qtost_fit$ci[k, ], alpha_qtost_fit$ci[k, ])
  estimate = c(qtost_fit$pi_y_hat[k], alpha_qtost_fit$pi_y_hat[k])
  cols = c("#501d8a", "#ee8c7d")
  ypos = c(2, 1)

  plot(NA, xlim = xlim, ylim = c(0.4, 2.7), axes = FALSE,
       xlab = expression(pi[y]), ylab = "", main = main)
  rect(pi_x - delta, 0.4, pi_x + delta, 2.7,
       col = adjustcolor("#FF9900", alpha.f = 0.15), border = NA)
  abline(h = ypos, col = "grey85")
  abline(v = pi_x, col = "grey65", lty = 3)
  abline(v = pi_x + c(-delta, delta), lty = 3)
  arrows(ci[, 1], ypos, ci[, 2], ypos, angle = 90, code = 3,
         length = 0.07, col = cols, lwd = 2.5)
  points(estimate, ypos, pch = 16, col = cols, cex = 1.5)
  axis(1)
  axis(2, at = ypos, labels = expression("qTOST", alpha*"-qTOST"),
       las = 1, tick = FALSE)
}

old_par = par(mfrow = c(2, 2), mar = c(4, 5.5, 2.5, 1), yaxs = "i")

for (i in seq_along(alphas)) {
  for (k in seq_along(pi_x)) {
    plot_intervals(lad_qtost[[i]], lad_alpha_qtost[[i]],
                   pi_x = pi_x[k], delta = delta, k = k,
                   xlim = if (k == 1) c(0, 0.6) else c(0.4, 1),
                   main = bquote(alpha == .(alphas[i]) ~ "," ~
                                 pi[x] == .(pi_x[k])))
  }
}
par(old_par)

Equivalence is established only when, at a given significance level, both intervals lie within their respective equivalence margins. Thus, neither procedure establishes joint equivalence at the 5% nominal level. At 10%, α\alpha-qTOST establishes joint equivalence, whereas qTOST does not.

References

Wu, J., Guerrier, S., Gou, S., Kalia, Y. N., and Insolia, L. (2025). Bridging the gap between experimental burden and statistical power for quantiles equivalence testing. arXiv:2510.17514.
